title: EF Core and data access in .NET
blurb: Tracking, loading strategies, concurrency, migrations in production, transactions and when to reach for Dapper.

questions.q: In EF Core 9 with default settings, what happens when this runs against a fresh DbContext?
choices: One extra query per order to fetch its customer: the classic N+1 problem
A NullReferenceException, because Customer was never loaded and stays null
EF notices the loop reads Customer and joins it into the first query for you
Blank lines, because EF fills Customer with an empty placeholder object
questions.why: Lazy loading is off by default in EF Core: it needs the Proxies package plus `UseLazyLoadingProxies()` and virtual navigations. Without it, an unloaded reference navigation is simply null. The N+1 answer describes what happens only when lazy loading is switched on. Load what you need up front with `Include` or, better, a projection.
questions.asked: Checks that you know EF Core defaults rather than EF6 or NHibernate habits, which is where most N+1 folklore comes from.

questions.q: A list page shows each order's number, date and customer name. Which query reads the least data?
choices: `db.Orders.Include(o => o.Customer).ToListAsync()`, joining the customer in
`db.Orders.AsNoTracking().Include(o => o.Customer).ToListAsync()`
`db.Orders.Select(o => new { o.Number, o.Date, o.Customer.Name }).ToListAsync()`
`db.Orders.ToListAsync()`, then `db.Customers.ToListAsync()` and a join in memory
questions.why: A projection becomes one SQL JOIN that selects exactly three columns, and the results are not tracked because they are not entities. `Include` fetches every column of both tables, with or without tracking. Loading both tables and joining in memory reads everything twice over. Project into a DTO for read-only screens and keep `Include` for when you will modify the graph.
questions.asked: The practical follow-up to "how do you avoid N+1": a strong answer reaches for projection, not only Include.

questions.q: Each blog has 200 posts and 50 tags. What does adding `AsSplitQuery()` to this query fix?
questions.code:
var blogs = await db.Blogs
    .Include(b => b.Posts)
    .Include(b => b.Tags)
    .ToListAsync();
choices: An N+1: without it, EF runs one query per blog to load its posts and its tags
Client evaluation: two Includes otherwise force EF to filter the rows in memory
Tracking overhead: split queries return untracked entities, which load faster
The JOIN returning 200 × 50 rows per blog: each collection gets its own query
questions.why: Two collection Includes in one query join into a cartesian product, so every blog comes back as 10,000 rows with its columns repeated. A split query loads blogs, posts and tags in three queries. The trade-off: more round trips, and without a transaction the separate queries can see different snapshots of the data. You can set split mode as the default with `UseQuerySplittingBehavior`.
questions.asked: Cartesian explosion is the performance bug that comes after you learn Include; knowing the consistency trade-off is the senior signal.

questions.q: Without lazy-loading proxies, how do you load the Lines of an order you already have, only when needed?
choices: `await db.Entry(order).Collection(o => o.Lines).LoadAsync()`
`await db.Entry(order).ReloadAsync()` with Lines declared virtual
`await db.Orders.Include(o => o.Lines).AttachAsync(order)`
`await order.Lines.LoadAsync()` called on the navigation itself
questions.why: Explicit loading goes through the entry: `Collection(...)` for collections, `Reference(...)` for single navigations, then `LoadAsync()`. It issues one query when you decide to, which is lazy loading made visible. `ReloadAsync` only refreshes scalar values from the database, and a navigation has no load method of its own. There is no `AttachAsync` on a query.
questions.asked: Shows you know the third loading strategy and can load conditionally without turning on proxies.

questions.q: The row with Id 1 has Name "Ann". In one tracking DbContext, what does this print?
choices: Ann: the second query creates a new instance, and both are now tracked
Ann: the second query refreshes the tracked entity from the database
changed: EF returns the instance it already tracks, without overwriting it
Nothing: it throws, because an entity with that key is already tracked
questions.why: A tracking context keeps one instance per key (identity resolution). The second query still runs SQL, but EF finds the key already tracked and returns the same instance without overwriting its values, so `b` and `a` are the same object. That is how unsaved edits survive a re-query. `AsNoTracking` would give a fresh object reading "Ann".
questions.asked: Tests whether you know the change tracker is also an identity map, which explains many "why did my query not see the database" bugs.

questions.q: When is `AsNoTracking()` the right choice?
choices: A query whose entities you will change and then save through the same context
A read-only query whose results you will not modify and save in this context
Any query that uses Include, because tracking does not work across joins
When two queries must return the same instance for the same database row
questions.why: No tracking skips the snapshot and identity bookkeeping, which is noticeably cheaper for lists, reports and API reads. The cost is that changes are not detected and you can get duplicate instances for the same row; `AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution` keeps one instance per key without tracking. Use tracking when you will modify and save.
questions.asked: An easy win to mention; the interviewer wants to hear when you would not use it, too.

questions.q: What does `SaveChangesAsync` write to the database here?
choices: An UPDATE of Status only, found by comparing the entity with the current row
An UPDATE of every column, because untracked entities are always fully rewritten
Nothing at all: the entity is not tracked, so the context detects no change
It throws, because an untracked entity was modified before SaveChanges ran
questions.why: SaveChanges only saves what the change tracker knows about, and `AsNoTracking` kept this entity out of it. The call succeeds and writes nothing, which is why this bug passes review. Remove `AsNoTracking` for queries you intend to modify, or call `Update`/`Attach` deliberately. EF never compares with the database row to find changes.
questions.asked: The "AsNoTracking everywhere" performance tip causes this bug; the interviewer wants to see you know the other side of it.

questions.q: You add an order and three lines, then call SaveChanges once. The third line violates a constraint. What is stored?
choices: The order and the first two lines, since each INSERT commits on its own
Nothing from this call: SaveChanges runs all its statements in one transaction
The order only, because the lines are saved in a second, separate transaction
Everything except the failing line, which EF skips and reports in the exception
questions.why: By default each SaveChanges call wraps its INSERTs, UPDATEs and DELETEs in a single transaction, so one failure rolls back the lot. That is why you should build a whole unit of work and save once. Work split across several SaveChanges calls is not atomic unless you begin a transaction yourself.
questions.asked: A basic guarantee that many candidates never realise they rely on.

questions.q: The row starts with IsActive = true. What does this print (EF Core 7+)?
choices: False, because EF refreshes the tracked copy of every row it updates
True, because ExecuteUpdate goes straight to SQL and ignores tracked entities
It throws, because rows cannot be bulk-updated while one of them is tracked
False, but only once SaveChangesAsync is called and flushes the tracker
questions.why: `ExecuteUpdate` and `ExecuteDelete` run a single SQL statement immediately, bypassing the change tracker and SaveChanges entirely. Entities already loaded keep their old values, so the tracker is now stale. Use them for set-based changes, and do not mix them with tracked edits of the same rows in one context without reloading.
questions.asked: Checks you know the modern bulk APIs and the trade-off: fast, but outside the unit of work.

questions.q: On SQL Server, what does this property on the Order entity do?
questions.code:
[Timestamp]
public byte[] RowVersion { get; set; } = null!;
choices: Stores the last-modified time in UTC so the edit screen can display it
Tells EF to lock the row with UPDLOCK whenever the order is read
Makes EF compare the original value of every column in each UPDATE
Maps to a rowversion column; EF adds it to each UPDATE's WHERE clause
questions.why: SQL Server bumps a `rowversion` value on every write. EF sends the value it read in the UPDATE's WHERE clause, so if someone else changed the row first, zero rows match and EF throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException. Despite the name it holds no time. This is optimistic concurrency, so nothing is locked on read.
questions.asked: Optimistic concurrency is the standard answer to lost updates in .NET; interviewers want the mechanism, not only the attribute.

questions.q: You move the app to PostgreSQL with Npgsql. What is the idiomatic replacement for the SQL Server rowversion token?
choices: Keep the `byte[]` property: Postgres has a native rowversion type
A `timestamptz` column defaulting to now(), which EF sets on each save
Nothing: Postgres detects conflicting updates on its own by default
This: a `uint` row version that Npgsql maps to the system column xmin
questions.why: Postgres has no rowversion type, but every row carries the system column `xmin`, which changes on each update. Npgsql maps a `uint` configured as a row version (or marked `[Timestamp]`) onto it, with no extra column. Postgres does not detect lost updates for you at the default isolation level. `[ConcurrencyCheck]` on an ordinary property is the provider-neutral alternative.
questions.asked: Separates people who copied a SQL Server tutorial from people who have shipped EF on more than one provider.

questions.q: An edit endpoint's SaveChanges throws `DbUpdateConcurrencyException`. What does that mean?
choices: Two threads used the same DbContext at the same time during the request
The database picked this transaction as the victim of a deadlock and aborted it
The UPDATE matched zero rows, because the token changed after the entity was read
Another transaction held a lock on the row until the command timeout expired
questions.why: EF checks the affected-row count. When the concurrency token in the WHERE clause no longer matches, the UPDATE affects nothing and EF raises this exception. The usual API response is 409 Conflict, so the client can reload and retry. Concurrent use of one context throws InvalidOperationException, and deadlocks and timeouts surface as provider exceptions.
questions.asked: The follow-up is "what does the client see?": a strong answer says 409 and a reload flow.

questions.q: User also has Name and CreatedAt columns. What does this PUT endpoint save?
choices: Only Email, because EF compares the new object with the stored row first
Every column: Name and CreatedAt are overwritten with null and default values
Nothing, because the newly created User instance was never tracked
An INSERT of a second user with the same Id, which fails on the primary key
questions.why: `Update` attaches the object and marks every property modified, so EF writes all columns from the object as it is, including the ones you never set. EF does not read the row first. Load the entity and copy the DTO onto it, or attach it and mark only `Email` as modified.
questions.asked: A real data-loss bug in CRUD code; the interviewer wants to hear "load, then apply".

questions.q: In EF Core 3 or later, what happens when this query runs?
choices: It loads every order and filters them in memory, logging a warning
EF inlines the body of IsRecent and translates the comparison to SQL
It returns an empty list, because unknown methods evaluate as false
It throws InvalidOperationException: the expression cannot be translated
questions.why: EF Core cannot see inside a compiled C# method, so it cannot translate `IsRecent` to SQL. Since EF Core 3 it throws instead of silently loading the whole table, which is what EF Core 2 did. Client evaluation is still allowed in the final `Select` projection. Write the condition inline, `o.CreatedAt > cutoff`, with `cutoff` computed before the query.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know where the SQL boundary is; the older silent client-evaluation behaviour still shows up in interview folklore.

questions.q: In EF Core 7 or later, which of these is safe against SQL injection?
questions.code:
var a = db.Users.FromSql($"SELECT * FROM Users WHERE Email = {email}");
var b = db.Users.FromSqlRaw("SELECT * FROM Users WHERE Email = '" + email + "'");
choices: `a`: FromSql turns each interpolated value into a DbParameter
`b`: FromSqlRaw escapes the quotes inside the concatenated string
Each of them: EF Core parameterises any SQL passed to a DbSet
Neither of them: raw SQL in EF Core is never parameterised
questions.why: `FromSql` (EF Core 7+, formerly `FromSqlInterpolated`) takes a FormattableString and sends every hole as a parameter. `FromSqlRaw` runs the string as given, so concatenating input into it is injectable. It is safe only with placeholders such as `{0}` plus separate arguments. The same rule applies to `ExecuteSql` and `ExecuteSqlRaw`.
questions.asked: The EF-specific version of the SQL injection question, and a common code review catch.

questions.q: With this filter configured, which query returns soft-deleted posts for an admin report?
questions.code: modelBuilder.Entity<Post>().HasQueryFilter(p => !p.IsDeleted);
choices: `db.Posts.AsNoTracking()`, because filters apply only to tracked queries
`db.Posts.IgnoreQueryFilters()`, which drops the filter for this query
`db.Set<Post>()`, because filters are bound to the `Posts` property only
`db.Posts.Where(p => p.IsDeleted)`, which overrides the model filter
questions.why: A global query filter is added to every query for that entity type, including Includes that load it through a navigation. Adding your own Where combines with it (AND), so `Where(p => p.IsDeleted)` returns nothing. Tracking and the way you reach the set make no difference. The same mechanism is used for per-tenant filtering.
questions.asked: Soft delete and multi-tenancy both rely on this; the strong answer mentions that filters apply to Includes too.

questions.q: What do you need before `dotnet ef migrations add Init` works in a new project?
choices: Only the database provider package, because the migration commands ship inside it
A running database, because EF diffs the live schema to generate the migration
The dotnet-ef tool, plus the Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Design package
A Visual Studio extension, because the CLI can apply migrations but not create them
questions.why: `dotnet ef` is a separate .NET tool (`dotnet tool install --global dotnet-ef`, or a local tool manifest), and it needs the Design package in the startup project to build and inspect your model. Adding a migration compares the model with the snapshot in your repository, not with a live database; only `database update` needs a connection.
questions.asked: Practical setup knowledge; the snapshot detail shows you know how migrations are generated.

questions.q: Why should an app that uses migrations not call `Database.EnsureCreated()` at startup?
choices: EnsureCreated drops and recreates the database each time the app starts
EnsureCreated applies pending migrations but skips the seed data they add
EnsureCreated works only on SQLite and throws for every other provider
It creates the schema without a migrations history, so migrations cannot follow
questions.why: `EnsureCreated` builds the schema straight from the current model and records no migrations history, so a later `Migrate()` tries to create tables that already exist. It also does nothing at all if the database exists, even when the model has changed. It suits throwaway test databases and prototypes; use migrations everywhere else.
questions.asked: Catches a common tutorial shortcut that breaks the first real schema change.

questions.q: What is the safest way to apply EF Core migrations to a production database?
choices: Call `Database.Migrate()` in Program.cs so each instance applies them on startup
Generate an idempotent SQL script or a migration bundle and run it as a deploy step
Run `dotnet ef database update` from a developer laptop against production
Let EnsureCreated add the missing tables and columns on the first request
questions.why: A script (`migrations script --idempotent`) or a bundle (`migrations bundle`) can be reviewed, run once by the pipeline with the right credentials, and fail before new code is live. Migrating at startup makes several instances race and gives the app schema-changing permissions. A laptop run is unrepeatable and unaudited.
questions.asked: Deployment maturity question; the interviewer is listening for "reviewable, run once, by the pipeline".

questions.q: A migration already applied in staging and production has a bug. What do you do?
choices: Edit the migration file to fix it, then run database update in every environment
Delete the migration and its snapshot changes, then add it again with the fix
Add a new migration that corrects the problem, and leave the applied one as it is
Run `migrations remove` so it is rolled back from every database it reached
questions.why: Databases record applied migrations by id in `__EFMigrationsHistory`, so an edited migration is never run again where it has already been applied, and environments silently diverge. Only migrations that have not left your machine are safe to change or remove. `migrations remove` only touches your code and refuses once the migration has been applied.
questions.asked: The same rule as "never rewrite published git history", applied to schema.

questions.q: How do you run two SaveChanges calls and an `ExecuteSqlAsync` as one unit at a chosen isolation level?
choices: Set `db.Database.IsolationLevel` once, and each SaveChanges call then uses it
Put a `[Transaction(IsolationLevel.Serializable)]` attribute on the endpoint
`db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync(level)`, then commit after all three calls
Nothing: all SaveChanges calls in one request already share a transaction
questions.why: EF exposes isolation only when you begin the transaction yourself; SaveChanges and raw SQL on that context then enlist in it until you commit or dispose. Otherwise each SaveChanges gets its own transaction at the database default. There is no per-context isolation property and no transaction attribute. What each level guarantees is a database question, not an EF one.
questions.asked: Checks you can make multi-step writes atomic, which comes up in every order or payment flow.

questions.q: With `EnableRetryOnFailure()`, `BeginTransactionAsync` throws "does not support user-initiated transactions". What is the fix?
choices: Remove the transaction, because the retries already make separate SaveChanges calls atomic
Run the whole transaction inside `db.Database.CreateExecutionStrategy().ExecuteAsync(...)`
Begin the transaction before the retry strategy is configured during application startup
Switch to a TransactionScope, because the retrying strategy is designed to ignore it
questions.why: A retrying strategy can only replay work it controls. If a transient failure happens halfway through your own transaction, retrying the last statement alone would be wrong, so EF refuses. Wrapping the whole block in the execution strategy lets it retry the transaction as one unit. TransactionScope is not supported with retries either.
questions.asked: Hits everyone who enables retries on Azure SQL; knowing the fix shows production EF experience.

questions.q: For which job is Dapper a better fit than EF Core?
choices: Editing an aggregate and its child rows through a form, then saving them together
Tracking changes to entities across several method calls before one final save
A hand-tuned reporting query whose exact SQL you want to write and control
Evolving the schema through versioned migrations checked into the repository
questions.why: Dapper maps the results of SQL you write onto objects, with almost no overhead, which suits reports, complex reads and stored procedures. It has no change tracking, unit of work or migrations, which are exactly what the other three jobs need. Many teams use both: EF Core for writes, Dapper for heavy reads.
questions.asked: Checks for tool judgement instead of tribal loyalty; "both, for different jobs" is the answer interviewers like.

questions.q: How does Dapper send `email` to the database here?
choices: As a parameter called @Email, taken from the anonymous object's property
Inlined into the SQL text after Dapper escapes any quotes it contains
As a parameter, but only when the SQL text is a stored procedure call
Positionally, in the order the properties appear in the anonymous object
questions.why: Dapper matches `@Email` to the property of the same name and sends a real DbParameter, so the query is injection-safe and its plan is reused. It never splices values into the text. The injection risk with Dapper comes only from building the SQL string itself with concatenation or interpolation.
questions.asked: Confirms you can use a micro-ORM without reintroducing SQL injection.

questions.q: What does `splitOn: "Id"` tell Dapper here?
choices: Which column to group rows by, so that each order appears only once
Which column is the key Dapper uses to track changes to each entity
Which column joins the two tables when Dapper rewrites the SQL text
Which column marks where the Customer's columns begin in each row
questions.why: Multi-mapping reads each flat row left to right and needs to know where one object ends and the next begins; `splitOn` names that boundary column ("Id" is the default). Dapper does no de-duplication, so an order with several lines in a one-to-many join comes back several times unless you group it yourself in the map function.
questions.asked: Only people who have used Dapper on joins know this; the one-to-many follow-up separates them further.

questions.q: A BackgroundService (a singleton) queries the database every minute. What is the idiomatic way to get a DbContext?
choices: Inject AppDb into its constructor, since the container scopes it per hosted service
Create one AppDb at startup and keep it in a static field for the service to reuse
Register AppDb as a singleton so that its lifetime matches the hosted service
Inject `IDbContextFactory<AppDb>` and create a short-lived context for each run
questions.why: `AddDbContextFactory` registers a factory that is safe to inject anywhere, and each run creates and disposes its own context, so the change tracker never grows or goes stale. Injecting the scoped context into a singleton is a captive dependency, and a long-lived shared context is not thread-safe. Creating a scope with `IServiceScopeFactory` also works.
questions.asked: Background jobs are where DbContext lifetime bugs show up; a strong answer names the factory or a scope.

questions.q: On PostgreSQL with Npgsql 6 or later, saving this entity throws 'Cannot write DateTime with Kind=Unspecified to PostgreSQL type timestamp with time zone'. Why?
choices: Npgsql maps `DateTime` to `timestamptz` and demands `Kind == Utc`; parse as UTC or use `DateTimeOffset`
Postgres has no `timestamp with time zone` type, so the column must be changed to `timestamp` in a migration
`DateTime.Parse` always yields Kind=Local, and Npgsql accepts only Local values for timestamptz columns
EF Core cannot translate `DateTime.Parse`, so the assignment must move into a `Select` projection instead
questions.why: Since Npgsql 6 a `DateTime` property maps to `timestamp with time zone` by default and only UTC values may be written, so an Unspecified or Local Kind is rejected instead of silently shifted. Parse with `DateTimeStyles.AdjustToUniversal`, use `DateTimeOffset`, or map the column to `timestamp without time zone` if it is genuinely a wall-clock value. The type exists in Postgres, and `DateTime.Parse` runs in C# before any SQL, so translation is not involved.
questions.asked: The most common EF-on-Postgres exception after a SQL Server migration; it tests whether you store instants or wall-clock times.

questions.q: With no attributes or Fluent API, which property does EF Core make the primary key of this entity?
choices: None: EF Core requires a `[Key]` attribute on one property
`Number`, because string keys are preferred when present
`InvoiceId`, because `<TypeName>Id` is a key by convention
A hidden shadow `Id` column that EF Core adds to the table
questions.why: EF Core treats a property named `Id` or `<type name>Id` as the key, and makes an integer key an identity column. `[Key]` or `HasKey` is needed only when your key breaks that convention. Without any key, EF refuses to map the type unless you mark it keyless.
questions.asked: A warm-up that checks you know what EF infers before you start configuring things.

questions.q: Nullable reference types are enabled. How does EF Core map these two properties in a migration?
questions.code:
public string Name { get; set; } = "";
public string? Notes { get; set; }
choices: Nullable for each, because strings are reference types in the database
NOT NULL for each, because EF Core ignores the `?` annotation entirely
`Name` nullable and `Notes` NOT NULL, the reverse of C# semantics
`Name` NOT NULL and `Notes` nullable, following the annotations
questions.why: With NRT enabled, EF Core reads the nullability annotations: a non-nullable `string` becomes a required column and `string?` an optional one. Before NRT, every string column was nullable unless marked `[Required]`, which is why older projects are full of that attribute.
questions.asked: Checks you know how C# nullability flows into the schema, a common source of surprise migrations.

questions.q: On SQL Server, what column type does EF Core create for a `string Title` property with no length configured?
choices: `nvarchar(max)`, unless you set a maximum length
`nvarchar(255)`, the length most ORMs choose
`varchar(50)`, to keep row sizes small by default
`text`, the legacy type used for long strings
questions.why: Unbounded strings map to `nvarchar(max)` on SQL Server (and `text` on Postgres, where it costs nothing). `nvarchar(max)` columns cannot be index keys and hide missing validation, so set `HasMaxLength` or `[MaxLength]` for things like names and emails.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to hear that you set lengths deliberately rather than living with the default.

questions.q: A property has `[MaxLength(100)]`, and `OnModelCreating` calls `HasMaxLength(200)` on it. What length does the column get?
choices: 100, because attributes always override code-based configuration
200, because the Fluent API is applied last and takes precedence
100, the smaller value, since EF picks the stricter of the two
Neither: EF throws at start-up because the settings conflict
questions.why: EF Core applies conventions, then data annotations, then the Fluent API, so explicit Fluent configuration wins. Many teams keep all mapping in `IEntityTypeConfiguration<T>` classes to avoid splitting it across two places.
questions.asked: Shows you know where the final model comes from when configuration is spread around.

questions.q: `Order` has an `int CustomerId` property and a `Customer` navigation, and `Customer` has `List<Order> Orders`. What must you configure for the relationship?
choices: Nothing: EF discovers the one-to-many relationship and the foreign key
`HasOne().WithMany()` in OnModelCreating, as EF never infers relationships
A `[ForeignKey]` attribute, because EF cannot guess which property is the key
A join table, because both sides have navigations to each other
questions.why: The navigations define a one-to-many relationship, and `CustomerId` matches the `<navigation>Id` naming convention, so it becomes the foreign key. Fluent configuration is only needed for non-standard names, delete behaviour or keys. Join tables are for many-to-many.
questions.asked: Establishes whether you rely on conventions knowingly or configure everything out of habit.

questions.q: In EF Core 5 or later, `Post` has `List<Tag> Tags` and `Tag` has `List<Post> Posts`, with no join class. What does a migration create?
choices: Nothing: EF Core cannot map many-to-many without a join entity
A `PostId` column on Tags and a `TagId` column on Posts
A join table with a composite key of the two foreign keys
A JSON column on Posts listing the Ids of every related tag
questions.why: Since EF Core 5, two collection navigations define a many-to-many relationship, and EF creates a join table (named `PostTag` by default) behind the scenes. You only need an explicit join entity when the link carries its own data.
questions.asked: A baseline relationships question; the follow-up is usually about join tables with extra columns.

questions.q: By default, how does EF Core store a C# enum property such as `OrderStatus Status`?
choices: As a string holding the member name, such as `Shipped`
As a separate lookup table with a foreign key to it
As its underlying integer value, such as 2
As a JSON object holding both the name and the number
questions.why: Enums map to their underlying integer type. `HasConversion<string>()` stores the names instead, which reads better in the database and survives reordering the enum, at the cost of wider columns. Renaming a member then becomes a data migration.
questions.asked: Leads into value converters and the trade-off between readable and compact storage.

questions.q: What does this configuration add to the schema?
choices: A check that runs in C# before SaveChanges, but nothing in the database
A unique index: the database rejects a second row with that email
An alternate key that other tables must reference instead of the Id
A non-unique index, with uniqueness enforced only on the next migration
questions.why: `HasIndex(...).IsUnique()` produces a unique index in the migration, so the database enforces the rule even under concurrent requests. EF Core does not check uniqueness in memory; a duplicate surfaces as a `DbUpdateException` from SaveChanges.
questions.asked: Uniqueness belongs in the database; interviewers check you don't rely on 'check then insert' alone.

questions.q: What is the point of this line in `OnModelCreating`?
questions.code: modelBuilder.ApplyConfigurationsFromAssembly(typeof(AppDbContext).Assembly);
choices: It scans the assembly for entities and adds a DbSet for each class it finds
It loads mapping from an XML file embedded as a resource in the assembly
It applies every migration class in the assembly to the database at start-up
It applies every `IEntityTypeConfiguration<T>` class found in the assembly
questions.why: Each entity's mapping can live in its own `IEntityTypeConfiguration<T>` class, and this call registers them all, keeping `OnModelCreating` short. It does not create DbSets, touch migrations or read XML.
questions.asked: Shows you have worked on a codebase large enough to organise mapping configuration.

questions.q: EF Core logs a warning that no store type was specified for a `decimal Price` property on SQL Server. What is the risk?
choices: It defaults to `decimal(18,2)`, so extra decimal places are silently lost
The column is created as `float`, so prices pick up binary rounding errors
The column is created as `nvarchar`, so prices sort alphabetically
The warning is cosmetic, because SQL Server stores any decimal exactly
questions.why: Without configuration EF uses `decimal(18,2)`, so a value like 1.2345 is rounded on save without an error. Set the precision with `HasPrecision(18, 4)` or `[Precision(18, 4)]` to match the business rule.
questions.asked: Money handling is a favourite interview topic; silent truncation is the trap to name.

questions.q: `Order` has a required foreign key to `Customer`. With default configuration, what happens when you delete a customer who has orders?
choices: The delete fails, because EF Core never deletes related rows
The orders are deleted too, since required relationships cascade
The orders stay, and their `CustomerId` values are set to null
The orders stay, pointing at a customer that no longer exists
questions.why: For required relationships EF Core defaults to `DeleteBehavior.Cascade`, both in the change tracker and in the foreign key it creates. That is often too aggressive for business data, so many teams switch to `Restrict` and delete or archive explicitly.
questions.asked: Cascade deletes can wipe data unexpectedly; interviewers like candidates who choose them on purpose.

questions.q: `Order.CouponId` is a nullable foreign key. With the default `ClientSetNull` behaviour, what happens when you delete a coupon?
choices: The database sets `CouponId` to null on every order that used the coupon
Every order that used the coupon is deleted along with it
EF nulls the FK on tracked orders; the database takes no action
EF loads every order that used the coupon and nulls each one in turn
questions.why: `ClientSetNull`, the default for optional relationships, fixes up only dependents the context is tracking; the database foreign key has no ON DELETE action. If untracked orders still reference the coupon, the delete fails with a constraint error. Use `SetNull` to have the database do it.
questions.asked: A subtle default that explains 'works in tests, fails in production' delete bugs.

questions.q: On SQL Server, a migration fails with 'may cause cycles or multiple cascade paths'. What is the usual fix?
choices: Set one relationship to `DeleteBehavior.Restrict` or `NoAction`
Switch the affected tables to a case-sensitive collation
Split the migration in two so the constraints are added separately
Remove the navigation properties so EF stops creating foreign keys
questions.why: SQL Server refuses a schema where one delete could cascade to a table along more than one path. Turning off cascade on one of the paths resolves it; you then delete those dependents yourself. Splitting the migration does not change the final schema.
questions.asked: A real SQL Server error most EF developers meet; knowing the fix shows experience.

questions.q: Students and courses are many-to-many, and you now need to store the date each student enrolled. How do you model it?
choices: Add an `EnrolledOn` property to Student and set it as each course is added
Add an `EnrolledOn` shadow property to the skip navigation's join table
Keep the skip navigations and store the date in a separate audit table
Add an `Enrollment` entity with both foreign keys and the date
questions.why: Once the link has data of its own it deserves an entity: `Enrollment` with `StudentId`, `CourseId` and `EnrolledOn`, mapped as the join entity so skip navigations can still be used. A property on Student can hold only one date for all courses.
questions.asked: Tests whether you can evolve a relationship when requirements add data to it.

questions.q: `Customer` configures `OwnsOne(c => c.ShippingAddress)`, where Address has Street and City. How is it stored by default?
choices: In a separate Addresses table with its own identity key
In the owner's table, as columns like `ShippingAddress_Street`
As one JSON column named `ShippingAddress` in the Customers table
As a single string that joins the street and city with commas
questions.why: Owned types are table-split into the owner's table by default, with columns named after the navigation and the property. You can move them to their own table with `ToTable`, or into a JSON column with `ToJson`, but neither is the default.
questions.asked: Owned types model value objects; interviewers check you know how they land in the schema.

questions.q: EF Core 8 added complex types (`ComplexProperty`). How do they differ from owned types?
choices: Complex types need their own table, while owned types share the owner's
Complex types can be queried through their own DbSet, owned types cannot
Complex types have no key and compare by value; owned types have one
Complex types are always stored as JSON, while owned types use columns
questions.why: Owned types are entities with a hidden key, tracked by identity, so one instance cannot be shared between owners. Complex types have no key and are compared by value, which fits value objects such as Money or Address. Both map to the owner's table by default.
questions.asked: A newer feature; knowing it signals you keep up with EF Core releases and understand value objects.

questions.q: `Order` has no `LastModified` property, but the model configures one. How do you filter on it in a query?
questions.code: modelBuilder.Entity<Order>().Property<DateTime>("LastModified");
choices: `db.Orders.Where(o => o.LastModified > since)`, since EF adds it to the class
`db.Orders.Where(o => EF.Property<DateTime>(o, "LastModified") > since)`
It cannot be queried, because shadow properties exist only in the change tracker
Through raw SQL only, because LINQ cannot reference columns without properties
questions.why: A shadow property exists in the model and the table but not on the CLR type. `EF.Property<T>(entity, name)` references it in LINQ, and `Entry(e).Property(name)` reads or sets it on tracked entities. EF does not add members to your class.
questions.asked: Shadow properties keep infrastructure columns out of domain classes; this checks you can still use them.

questions.q: How does EF Core populate `Lines` when loading an order with `Include(o => o.Lines)`?
choices: It fails, because the navigation has no setter for EF to assign
It creates a new list and ignores `_lines`, so the lines vanish
It adds lines only when `Lines` is cast back to a `List<OrderLine>`
It finds the `_lines` backing field by convention and fills it
questions.why: EF Core matches backing fields by naming convention (`_lines` for `Lines`) and reads and writes the field directly. That lets a domain class expose a read-only collection while EF still materialises and tracks it.
questions.asked: Encapsulated collections are common in DDD-leaning codebases; this checks EF can work with them.

questions.q: In EF Core 7+ on SQL Server, what does this configuration do with an order's list of gift options?
questions.code:
modelBuilder.Entity<Order>()
    .OwnsMany(o => o.GiftOptions, b => b.ToJson());
choices: Stores the whole list in one JSON column that queries can still reach
Serialises the list to JSON in memory but never saves it to the database
Creates a GiftOptions table and returns its rows to clients as JSON
Stores the list as XML, because SQL Server has no JSON column support
questions.why: `ToJson` maps an owned type or collection to a single JSON column, and EF translates LINQ over it into SQL Server's JSON functions. It suits data always read with its owner; relational tables are still better for data you join, index or constrain.
questions.asked: JSON columns are a modern modelling option; interviewers want to hear when not to use them too.

questions.q: On SQL Server, EF Core creates this unique index for a nullable `Email` column. What does it add to it?
questions.code: modelBuilder.Entity<User>().HasIndex(u => u.Email).IsUnique();
choices: Nothing: only one row may have a null Email, as SQL Server treats nulls as equal
A filter `[Email] IS NOT NULL`, so many rows can have no email
A case-sensitive collation, so emails differing in case stay distinct
An INCLUDE clause covering every other column of the Users table
questions.why: SQL Server's unique indexes allow only one NULL, so EF Core adds an `IS NOT NULL` filter for unique indexes on nullable columns. You can set your own filter with `HasFilter`, for example to ignore soft-deleted rows.
questions.asked: Filtered indexes show you know how provider quirks shape the schema EF generates.

questions.q: In EF Core 7+, how do you declare a composite primary key for this join entity?
choices: Put `[Key]` on both properties; EF combines them in declaration order
Name one property `Id`, and EF adds the other to the key automatically
`HasKey(l => new { l.OrderId, l.ProductId })`, or `[PrimaryKey]`
Composite keys are unsupported, so add a surrogate `Id` column instead
questions.why: `HasKey` with an anonymous type defines a composite key, and EF Core 7 added the class-level `[PrimaryKey(nameof(OrderId), nameof(ProductId))]` attribute. Putting `[Key]` on two properties is an error in EF Core, unlike EF6.
questions.asked: Composite keys appear in every join table; this checks you can configure them in modern EF.

questions.q: `Card` and `BankTransfer` inherit from `Payment`, and only `Payment` has a DbSet. With no inheritance configuration, what schema does EF Core create?
choices: One table per class, joined on the key when a payment is loaded
One table per concrete class, with no table for the base class
One table, with a `Discriminator` column naming the type
Only a Payments table, and derived properties are not stored
questions.why: Table-per-hierarchy is the default: every type shares one table, subtype columns are nullable, and a `Discriminator` column says which class each row is. TPT and TPC must be opted into with `UseTptMappingStrategy` or `UseTpcMappingStrategy`.
questions.asked: Inheritance mapping comes up whenever a domain has variants; knowing the default is the start.

questions.q: `IsActive` is configured with `HasDefaultValue(true)`. What does this save, and why does EF Core warn about it?
questions.code:
db.Users.Add(new User { Name = "Ann", IsActive = false });
await db.SaveChangesAsync();
choices: `IsActive = false`, because an explicit value always overrides a default
`IsActive = true`: false is the CLR default, so EF leaves it out
Nothing: SaveChanges throws because the value conflicts with the default
`IsActive = null`, because the database default replaces the value sent
questions.why: EF treats the CLR default (the 'sentinel', `false` for bool) as 'not set' and leaves the column out of the INSERT, so the database default of true wins. Make the property `bool?`, give it a different sentinel with `HasSentinel`, or drop the database default.
questions.asked: A classic subtle bug; spotting it shows you understand how EF decides which columns to send.

questions.q: What is the main trade-off between the TPT and TPC inheritance strategies?
choices: TPT joins to load a subtype; TPC avoids that, but base queries use UNION
TPT stores every subtype in one table; TPC splits them into one table each
TPT supports identity keys across subtypes; TPC forbids keys on base types
TPT works only with SQL Server, while TPC works only with PostgreSQL
questions.why: TPT puts base columns in one table and subtype columns in others, so loading a subtype joins them. TPC gives each concrete type a full table, which is fast for single types but needs UNION for base-type queries and key generation that is unique across tables, such as a shared sequence.
questions.asked: A deeper modelling question; strong answers relate the choice to how the data is queried.

questions.q: On PostgreSQL, why might a team generate Guid keys with `Guid.CreateVersion7()` (.NET 9) rather than `Guid.NewGuid()`?
choices: Version 7 Guids are shorter, so they fit in a 64-bit bigint column
Version 7 Guids are guaranteed unique across servers, unlike version 4
PostgreSQL rejects random version 4 values in columns of type `uuid`
Version 7 values are time-ordered, so inserts append to the index
questions.why: Random v4 values scatter inserts across the primary key's B-tree, causing page splits and poor cache use on large tables. UUIDv7 starts with a timestamp, so inserts append like an identity column while keeping client-side key generation. Both are 128-bit and practically unique.
questions.asked: Key choice affects write performance at scale; this checks you know why, not just the rule.

questions.q: `Status` is an enum stored as a string with `HasConversion<string>()`. What does `OrderBy(o => o.Status)` sort by?
choices: The enum's numeric values, because EF converts back before sorting
The declaration order of the enum members, as C# would compare them
The stored names alphabetically, because SQL sorts the column text
Nothing: ordering on a converted property throws a translation error
questions.why: Queries run in SQL against the stored representation, so a string-converted enum sorts alphabetically (Cancelled, Pending, Shipped) and range comparisons use string order too. Store numbers or add an explicit sort column if order matters.
questions.asked: Value converters have query-time consequences; this checks you think past the mapping line.

questions.q: What does configuring a key with `UseHiLo()` on SQL Server change?
choices: EF reserves blocks of ids from a sequence, saving a round trip per key
EF switches the key to a Guid so ids can be created without the database
The database assigns keys in descending order to spread index writes
EF uses a table lock during inserts so identity values have no gaps
questions.why: Hi-Lo fetches a range of values from a database sequence and hands them out in memory, so EF knows keys before INSERT and can batch dependents without reading identities back. The cost is gaps and a sequence to manage.
questions.asked: A less common but telling option: it shows you know how key generation affects batching.

questions.q: You run `dotnet ef migrations add AddPhone`. Which files does it create or change?
choices: Only a .sql file with the ALTER TABLE statements to run by hand
A migration with Up and Down, a designer file, and the snapshot
The database itself, which is altered as soon as the command finishes
Only the model snapshot, since migrations are computed when applied
questions.why: The command compares the current model with the snapshot, writes a migration class with `Up` and `Down`, a `.Designer.cs` with metadata, and updates `<Context>ModelSnapshot.cs`. It does not touch the database; `dotnet ef database update` or a script does that.
questions.asked: A starter question that shows whether you have used migrations or only read about them.

questions.q: How does `dotnet ef database update` know which migrations a database already has?
choices: It compares the live schema with the model and diffs every table
It reads a `.migrations` file stored next to the connection string
It reads the applied ids from the `__EFMigrationsHistory` table
It asks the developer which migration to start from each time
questions.why: Each applied migration inserts its id into `__EFMigrationsHistory`, and EF applies the ones missing from that table in order. It never diffs the live schema, which is why manual schema changes drift silently from the model.
questions.asked: Knowing the history table helps you debug 'migration already applied' and drift problems.

questions.q: You added a migration locally but have not applied it anywhere. How do you undo it cleanly?
choices: Delete the migration's .cs files and leave the snapshot as it is
Run `dotnet ef database update 0` to wipe the migration from disk
Add another migration that reverses the changes made by the first
Run `dotnet ef migrations remove`; it also reverts the snapshot
questions.why: `migrations remove` deletes the last migration and restores the snapshot to its previous state. Deleting files by hand leaves the snapshot ahead of the migrations, so the next migration misses changes. Once a migration is applied to shared databases, add a new one instead.
questions.asked: Checks you can iterate on a migration before sharing it without corrupting the snapshot.

questions.q: What is the `Down` method of a migration for?
choices: Undoing the changes when you update to an earlier migration
Running after `Up` to clean up any temporary tables it created
Seeding data after the schema changes in `Up` are applied
Checking the database is reachable before `Up` starts
questions.why: `Down` undoes `Up`, and runs when you target an earlier migration, for example `dotnet ef database update AddOrders`. It is generated for you but not always lossless: dropping a column in `Down` loses data added since, which is why production teams usually roll forward.
questions.asked: Leads into the roll-back versus roll-forward conversation.

questions.q: What does `HasData` in `OnModelCreating` do with this lookup data?
choices: Inserts the rows each time the app starts, if they are not there yet
Uses the rows only in tests, never in a real database
Puts the rows in migrations, which insert, update or delete them
Caches the rows in memory so queries skip the database
questions.why: `HasData` makes seed rows part of the model, so migrations contain `InsertData`, `UpdateData` or `DeleteData` when they change. It suits static reference data with fixed keys; it does not run at start-up and needs explicit key values.
questions.asked: Distinguishes model seed data from runtime seeding, a common confusion.

questions.q: In Program.cs, where does this connection string come from with the default builder?
questions.code:
builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(o =>
    o.UseNpgsql(builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("Default")));
choices: Only from a file named connectionstrings.json in the project root
The `ConnectionStrings:Default` key from any configuration source
The `Default` entry of the machine's ODBC data source list
An environment variable named exactly `Default`, and nowhere else
questions.why: `GetConnectionString(name)` is shorthand for `configuration["ConnectionStrings:name"]`, so appsettings, user secrets or an environment variable `ConnectionStrings__Default` can all supply it. Keep real credentials out of committed appsettings files.
questions.asked: Basic wiring; the follow-up is usually where you keep the production secret.

questions.q: Your local database has migrations up to `AddInvoices`. How do you return it to the state after `AddCustomers`, an earlier migration?
choices: `dotnet ef migrations remove AddCustomers`
`dotnet ef database update AddCustomers`
`dotnet ef database drop --to AddCustomers`
`dotnet ef migrations reset AddCustomers`
questions.why: `database update <target>` runs the `Down` methods of every later migration until the database matches the target. `migrations remove` only deletes the newest migration's files; `database drop` deletes the whole database.
questions.asked: Checks you can move a development database between states while working on branches.

questions.q: You add a required `string Sku` property to a table that already has rows. What does the generated migration do?
choices: Adds the column as nullable, ignoring the entity's annotations
Fails to generate, because a required column needs existing data
Drops and recreates the table so every row gets a fresh value
Adds a NOT NULL column with a default such as an empty string
questions.why: EF scaffolds `AddColumn` with `nullable: false` and `defaultValue: ""`, so existing rows get an empty string. That satisfies the constraint but may not be valid data; edit the migration to backfill real values when it matters.
questions.asked: Tests whether you read generated migrations instead of trusting them blindly.

questions.q: What is the `<Context>ModelSnapshot.cs` file used for?
choices: It records the model at the last migration, to diff the next one
It stores a copy of the production data for use in local testing
It caches compiled queries so that the app starts faster in production
It lists the migrations applied to each environment's database
questions.why: When you add a migration, EF compares the current model with the snapshot rather than with a database, then updates the snapshot. The applied-migrations list lives in `__EFMigrationsHistory` in each database, not in source.
questions.asked: Understanding the snapshot is the key to resolving migration merge conflicts.

questions.q: With Npgsql's EF Core provider and default settings, why does raw SQL `SELECT * FROM Orders` fail while EF queries work?
choices: Npgsql blocks raw SQL unless `AllowRawSql` is enabled in options
PostgreSQL requires a schema prefix, so it must be `public.Orders`
EF quotes the name `"Orders"`; unquoted names fold to lower case
EF creates the table under a random name and maps it internally
questions.why: EF quotes identifiers, so the table is literally `Orders`; PostgreSQL folds unquoted identifiers to lower case and looks for `orders`. Quote names in raw SQL, or use a snake_case naming convention (for example EFCore.NamingConventions) so no quoting is needed.
questions.asked: A classic first day on Postgres with EF; it shows you understand identifier case rules.

questions.q: You rename `Customer.Name` to `FullName` and add a migration. What does EF Core scaffold, and what should you do?
choices: A `RenameColumn`, since EF tracks property renames through the snapshot
A drop of `Name` and an add of `FullName`; edit it to `RenameColumn`
Nothing, because column names are fixed once the table is created
A new `FullName` column, keeping `Name` so no data is ever lost
questions.why: The snapshot only sees one property disappear and another appear, so the migration drops `Name` (losing data) and adds `FullName`. Replace the two operations with `migrationBuilder.RenameColumn`. Always review generated migrations for destructive steps.
questions.asked: A common way to lose production data; interviewers want to hear that you read migrations.

questions.q: Two branches each add a migration. After merging, the model snapshot has a conflict. What is the safest resolution?
choices: Keep either side of the snapshot, as EF regenerates it on the next full build
Delete the snapshot file; EF rebuilds it from the database on demand
Resolve the snapshot to hold both changes, then check with a new migration
Merge the two migrations into one file, then delete both designer files
questions.why: The snapshot must reflect the combined model. Take both sides' changes (or remove your migration, merge, and re-add it), then run `migrations add` to confirm it generates nothing unexpected. EF never regenerates the snapshot from a database or build.
questions.asked: Teams hit this weekly; knowing the process separates solo from team experience.

questions.q: What does the `--idempotent` flag change about this command's output?
questions.code: dotnet ef migrations script --idempotent -o migrate.sql
choices: Each migration is wrapped in a check against the history table
The script drops and recreates the database so reruns match
The script contains only the latest migration, not all of them
Every statement runs twice to confirm the result is identical
questions.why: An idempotent script guards each migration with a check on `__EFMigrationsHistory`, so it can run against a database at any earlier migration and apply only what is missing. That suits pipelines that do not know the target's current state.
questions.asked: SQL scripts are the reviewable way to deploy migrations; idempotency makes them safe to rerun.

questions.q: What does `dotnet ef migrations bundle` produce?
choices: A NuGet package holding the migrations for other projects to reference
A zip of the migration .cs files for attaching to a pull request
A Docker image that runs the database with migrations pre-applied
An executable that applies migrations without the SDK or source code
questions.why: A bundle (`efbundle`) is a self-contained executable that takes a connection string and applies pending migrations, which suits deployment pipelines where the build output, not the repo, reaches the server.
questions.asked: Shows familiarity with deployment options beyond running `database update` from a laptop.

questions.q: After upgrading to EF Core 9, `db.Database.Migrate()` throws about pending model changes. What does it mean?
choices: The database has migrations that are missing from the assembly
The model has changed since the last migration; add one
Another instance holds the migration lock, so this one gave up
The connection string points at a database EF did not create
questions.why: EF Core 9 turns the pending-model-changes warning into an error when migrating, so you cannot ship a model change without its migration. Add the missing migration; in CI, `dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes` catches it earlier.
questions.asked: A real upgrade surprise; it checks you keep the model and migrations in step.

questions.q: Why is `HasData` a poor fit for seeding a demo admin user with a hashed password generated at runtime?
choices: Seed values live in the model, so runtime values cause churn migrations
`HasData` cannot seed tables that have a string primary key column
`HasData` rows are deleted on each start-up, so the admin account would vanish
`HasData` requires every column to be nullable in the target table
questions.why: `HasData` values are compared on every `migrations add`, so a value computed at runtime (a new hash, `DateTime.Now`, a new Guid) produces a new migration every time. Use `UseSeeding`/`UseAsyncSeeding` (EF Core 9) or start-up code for data that is not static.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know the limits of model seeding and the modern alternative.

questions.q: When does a project need an `IDesignTimeDbContextFactory<AppDbContext>`?
choices: Always: EF Core cannot generate migrations without one
When the app runs in production with pooled DbContexts
When the tools cannot build the context through the app's host
When the DbContext has more than one constructor overload
questions.why: The tools usually create the context through the application's service provider. If the context lives in a class library, or start-up needs things unavailable at design time, a design-time factory tells the tools how to construct it.
questions.asked: Comes up whenever data access sits in its own project; it shows you understand how the tools work.

questions.q: A migration adds a `Status` column, and existing rows must get a value computed from other columns. Where does that logic go?
choices: In a SaveChanges override that fixes up each row the next time it is saved
In `HasDefaultValueSql`, since defaults can read other columns of the row
In a background job the app starts after every deployment
In the migration: `migrationBuilder.Sql("UPDATE ...")` after `AddColumn`
questions.why: Migrations can carry data changes: add the column, run an `UPDATE` with `migrationBuilder.Sql`, then tighten constraints if needed. The backfill then runs exactly once per database, in order with the schema change. Column defaults cannot reference other columns.
questions.asked: Real migrations include data; interviewers check you know migrations are not only schema.

questions.q: The same `Where(u => u.Email == email)` query finds `Ann@Example.com` for input `ann@example.com` on SQL Server but not on PostgreSQL. Why?
choices: Npgsql lower-cases parameters, while SQL Server leaves them unchanged
SQL Server's usual collation ignores case; PostgreSQL's does not
EF Core evaluates string equality in memory on PostgreSQL only
PostgreSQL trims and lower-cases text columns when rows are inserted
questions.why: The comparison runs in the database, so collation decides. SQL Server's usual default collation ignores case; PostgreSQL's does not. Normalise emails when saving, or use a case-insensitive collation or `citext` column on Postgres.
questions.asked: Provider differences like this break apps during migrations between databases.

questions.q: On SQL Server, what does `ToTable(t => t.IsTemporal())` give an entity?
questions.code: modelBuilder.Entity<Price>().ToTable(t => t.IsTemporal());
choices: A history table the database fills, queryable with `TemporalAsOf`
A table that SQL Server deletes automatically when the connection closes
A copy of each row in memory for the lifetime of the DbContext
Automatic soft delete, with rows flagged instead of removed
questions.why: Temporal tables keep every previous version of a row in a history table maintained by the database. EF Core maps them and exposes `TemporalAsOf`, `TemporalAll` and similar operators to query past states, which is handy for audit questions.
questions.asked: A useful feature for audit requirements; knowing it exists can save building history by hand.

questions.q: What does `dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes` (EF Core 8+) let a CI pipeline check?
choices: That every migration has already been applied to the production database
That no migration drops a column or table holding data
That the model has changes without a migration, failing the build
That migrations from different branches do not conflict
questions.why: The command exits with an error when the model differs from the latest snapshot, so a forgotten migration fails the build rather than production. It does not connect to a database or inspect migrations for destructive steps.
questions.asked: Shows you automate the checks that stop broken deployments.

questions.q: Migrations live in a separate `Shop.Migrations` project. What must the context's options say?
choices: `UseMigrationsFolder("Shop.Migrations")` pointing at the folder
Nothing: EF scans every loaded assembly for migration classes
`MigrationsAssembly("Shop.Migrations")` in the provider options
`[assembly: Migrations]` added to the app's Program.cs
questions.why: By default EF expects migrations in the assembly containing the DbContext. `o.UseSqlServer(cs, x => x.MigrationsAssembly("Shop.Migrations"))` tells it where to look, which also lets you keep per-provider migration projects.
questions.asked: Relevant for multi-project solutions and apps that support more than one database.

questions.q: Three instances of an API call `Database.Migrate()` at start-up at the same moment. What does EF Core 9 add to help?
choices: Nothing: the instances race, and duplicate migrations can be applied
It skips migration on every instance except the one with the lowest IP
It retries each migration until all three instances report success
A database lock, so one instance migrates while the others wait
questions.why: EF Core 9 takes a database-level lock around migration so concurrent `Migrate` calls do not apply the same migration twice. Even so, many teams apply migrations in a pipeline step rather than at start-up, so failures do not crash every instance.
questions.asked: Tests awareness of multi-instance deployment hazards and recent EF improvements.

questions.q: You must rename a column used by a live API with rolling deployments and no downtime. What is the usual approach?
choices: Expand/contract: add, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, drop later
A single `RenameColumn` migration deployed together with the new code
Rename the column in a transaction so old instances wait until it commits
Stop the old instances first, rename, then start the new ones immediately
questions.why: During a rolling deployment old and new code run side by side, so the schema must suit both. Expand (add the new column and write to both), migrate data, switch reads, then contract (drop the old column) in a later release. A plain rename breaks the old instances instantly.
questions.asked: A senior-leaning question that shows you think about deployments, not just schema.

questions.q: You need a NOT NULL `Region` column on a 200-million-row table. Why not ship one migration that adds it with a computed backfill?
choices: EF Core cannot generate migrations for tables over 100 million rows
NOT NULL columns can only be added to empty tables in any database
One huge UPDATE can hold locks and bloat the log; do it in stages
The backfill would run on every app start-up rather than once
questions.why: A single statement touching every row can lock the table, fill the transaction log and time out. Add the column as nullable, backfill in batches outside a long transaction, then add the NOT NULL constraint once every row has a value.
questions.asked: Checks you plan migrations around data volume, not just correctness.

questions.q: A project has 300 migrations and new developers wait minutes for their database. What is a reasonable way to squash them?
choices: Replace them with one baseline, marked as applied on existing databases
Delete `__EFMigrationsHistory` everywhere so EF regenerates it automatically
Combine every migration's Up body into a new migration and keep the old files
Switch to `EnsureCreated()` for every environment, including production
questions.why: A new baseline migration creates the current schema for fresh databases; existing databases need its id inserted into `__EFMigrationsHistory` so it is not reapplied. Clearing history makes EF try to rerun everything, and `EnsureCreated` cannot evolve a schema.
questions.asked: Long-lived projects need this; a careful answer shows you understand what the history table does.

questions.q: On PostgreSQL, you want email lookups to ignore case while keeping an index usable. Which approach fits?
choices: Call `ToLower()` on the parameter only, leaving the column as it is
Use a case-insensitive column type or collation, such as `citext`
Wrap the query in `AsEnumerable()` and compare with `StringComparison`
Set `EnableSensitiveDataLogging(false)` so casing is ignored
questions.why: A `citext` column (or a nondeterministic collation, or an index on `lower(email)` queried the same way) makes the database compare without case and still use an index. Lowering only the parameter misses mixed-case stored values, and `AsEnumerable` loads the whole table.
questions.asked: Combines provider knowledge with performance; strong answers mention index usage.

questions.q: What does this code send to the database?
questions.code:
IEnumerable<Order> orders = db.Orders;
var big = orders.Where(o => o.Total > 1000).ToList();
choices: A query with `WHERE Total > 1000`, like any LINQ query on a DbSet
Nothing until `Where` runs, then one query per matching order
A query for every order; the filter then runs in memory
An error, because a DbSet cannot be assigned to IEnumerable
questions.why: Typing the variable as `IEnumerable<T>` makes `Where` bind to LINQ to Objects, so EF only sees 'give me all orders' and filtering happens in C#. Keep queries as `IQueryable<T>` until they are complete so EF can translate the whole thing.
questions.asked: The IQueryable/IEnumerable boundary is the root of many slow endpoints.

questions.q: When does this query actually run against the database?
choices: On the first line, when `Where` is called on the DbSet
When `ToListAsync` is awaited, since the query is deferred
When `count` is declared, as EF runs queries on the next statement
Twice: once when it is built and once for `ToListAsync`
questions.why: LINQ over `IQueryable` builds an expression; nothing runs until something enumerates it, such as `ToListAsync`, `FirstAsync`, `CountAsync` or a `foreach`. That lets you compose filters conditionally before executing once.
questions.asked: Deferred execution is fundamental; interviewers check you know when the SQL happens.

questions.q: What is different about `db.Products.FindAsync(id)` compared with `FirstOrDefaultAsync(p => p.Id == id)`?
choices: `FindAsync` checks entities the context already tracks before querying
`FindAsync` bypasses global query filters and returns deleted rows too
`FindAsync` always queries the database, ignoring anything already tracked
`FindAsync` loads all navigation properties of the entity automatically
questions.why: `Find` looks up the primary key in the change tracker first and only queries when the entity is not there, so repeated lookups in one context are free. It works by key only and does not load navigations. `FirstOrDefault` always runs a query.
questions.asked: A small API detail that shows you know the change tracker doubles as an identity map.

questions.q: What happens when `SingleOrDefaultAsync(u => u.Email == email)` finds two matching rows?
choices: It returns the first of the two, in primary key order
It returns null, as it would for no match at all
It throws InvalidOperationException
It returns whichever row the database happens to send back first
questions.why: `Single` asks for two rows (`TOP(2)` or `LIMIT 2`) so it can detect duplicates, and throws when it gets more than one. `First` would take one silently. Use `Single` when duplicates mean corrupt data and you want to hear about it.
questions.asked: Choosing between First and Single signals whether you think about data invariants.

questions.q: Why prefer `await db.Orders.AnyAsync(o => o.CustomerId == id)` over `CountAsync(...) > 0` to check existence?
choices: `AnyAsync` caches the answer for the lifetime of the context
`CountAsync` loads every matching row into memory before counting
`AnyAsync` is the only form that works with global query filters
`AnyAsync` becomes EXISTS, which can stop at the first match
questions.why: `Any` translates to `EXISTS (...)`, so the database can stop after one row; `COUNT` must count every match. Both run in SQL; neither loads rows into memory or caches results.
questions.asked: A simple habit that shows you think about the SQL your LINQ produces.

questions.q: EF Core warns about this paging query. Why?
choices: Skip and Take must come before Where, or the SQL will not compile
Without OrderBy, row order is undefined, so pages can overlap
Take(20) is ignored unless AsNoTracking is added to the query
Skip is evaluated in memory, so all rows are loaded first
questions.why: Databases guarantee no order without `ORDER BY`, so the same page can return different rows between calls. Order by something unique (add the key as a tie-breaker). EF translates Skip and Take to OFFSET/FETCH or LIMIT/OFFSET in SQL.
questions.asked: Paging bugs are common in list screens; this is the first thing reviewers check.

questions.q: How does EF Core handle this query when `ids` is a `List<int>` with 50 values?
choices: It loads every order and filters by the list in memory
It sends 50 queries, one for each id in the list
It throws, because local lists cannot be used in queries
It sends one query matching the ids with an IN-style filter
questions.why: `Contains` on a local collection translates to SQL, passing the values as parameters (EF Core 8+ may send the list as one JSON or array parameter, depending on provider and version). It is the standard way to fetch a batch of rows by id.
questions.asked: Fetching by a list of ids is everyday work; knowing it stays in SQL avoids workarounds.

questions.q: In an ASP.NET Core endpoint, why use `await db.Orders.ToListAsync()` rather than `db.Orders.ToList()`?
choices: The async version runs the SQL faster on the database server
The async version frees the request thread while waiting on I/O
The sync version is unsupported by EF Core and throws at runtime
The async version caches results between requests automatically
questions.why: While the database works, an async call returns the thread to the pool so it can serve other requests; a blocking call holds it. The query is no faster, but under load the app scales much better. Both are supported.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know what async buys a web server, not just that it is 'better'.

questions.q: What is the quickest way to see the SQL that EF Core will run for a LINQ query while debugging?
choices: Call `.ToQueryString()` on the IQueryable
Call `.ToString()` on the result of ToListAsync
Read `db.Database.LastCommandText` after it runs
Open the model snapshot to find the generated SQL
questions.why: `ToQueryString()` returns the SQL for an `IQueryable` without running it, including parameter declarations. For running queries, configure logging with `LogTo` or the `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command` log category.
questions.asked: Reading generated SQL is the first step in any EF performance investigation.

questions.q: An endpoint returns customer summaries. Why is this better than returning the `Customer` entities?
questions.code: db.Customers.Select(c => new CustomerSummary(c.Id, c.Name, c.Orders.Count))
choices: Projections are the only queries EF Core can run without tracking
Entities cannot be serialised to JSON by System.Text.Json at all
Returning entities makes EF write any changes back on serialisation
It reads only needed columns and hides internal fields from the API
questions.why: A projection selects just the columns the DTO needs (with the count done in SQL), keeps the API contract separate from the table, and avoids leaking fields like password hashes or causing serialisation cycles. Projections are also untracked automatically.
questions.asked: DTO versus entity is a standard API design question with a performance angle.

questions.q: Why do large product lists often switch from `Skip/Take` to keyset (seek) pagination?
questions.code:
db.Products.Where(p => p.Id > lastId)
  .OrderBy(p => p.Id).Take(20)
choices: OFFSET is unsupported by PostgreSQL, so Skip fails there
Keyset paging lets the client jump straight to any page number
Deep OFFSETs still read skipped rows; a seek starts at the key
Skip/Take loads each page into memory before trimming it
questions.why: `OFFSET 100000` makes the database walk and discard 100,000 rows, getting slower with depth, and inserts shift pages. Seeking on an indexed key reads just the next rows and stays stable. The cost is no random access to page N.
questions.asked: Shows you know how paging behaves at scale and the trade-off in UX.

questions.q: What does the `Include` do in this query?
questions.code:
var rows = await db.Orders
    .Include(o => o.Lines)
    .Select(o => new { o.Id, o.Total })
    .ToListAsync();
choices: It loads every order's lines too, then discards them after the query
It adds a JOIN to Lines, so each order appears once per line
It throws, because Include cannot be combined with a projection
Nothing: the projection decides what is loaded, so it is ignored
questions.why: When a query ends in a projection, EF loads exactly what the projection references; `Include` only affects queries that return entity types. Remove it to avoid confusing readers, or reference the lines in the projection if you need them.
questions.asked: A common redundant pattern in code reviews; knowing why it is ignored shows understanding.

questions.q: What does this EF Core 5+ query load?
questions.code: db.Blogs.Include(b => b.Posts.Where(p => p.IsPublished))
choices: Every blog, with only its published posts in the Posts collection
Only blogs that have at least one published post, with all posts
Every blog and every post, filtered later when Posts is enumerated
An error, because Include accepts only a plain navigation property
questions.why: Filtered include applies the condition to the related collection only; it does not filter the blogs. Beware: if the context already tracks other posts for those blogs, fix-up can add them to the collection too.
questions.asked: Filtered include is newer and easily confused with filtering the parent rows.

questions.q: How do you load each order's lines and each line's product in one query?
choices: `Include(o => o.Lines.Product)` with a dotted property path
`Include(o => o.Lines).ThenInclude(l => l.Product)`
`Include(o => o.Lines).Include(o => o.Product)`
`Include("Product").Include("Lines")` in either order
questions.why: `ThenInclude` continues from the previous navigation, so it can step through a collection to each element's reference. `Lines.Product` does not compile because `Lines` is a collection, and a second `Include` starts again from `Order`.
questions.asked: Everyday syntax for multi-level loading; the follow-up is usually about projecting instead.

questions.q: On SQL Server, why can this search be slow on a large table even with an index on `Name`?
questions.code: db.Products.Where(p => p.Name.Contains(term))
choices: `Contains` is evaluated in memory after loading every product
It becomes `LIKE '%term%'`; a leading wildcard rules out a seek
`Contains` makes SQL Server rebuild the index on every single query
The term is inlined as a literal, so each search compiles a new plan
questions.why: `string.Contains` translates to a LIKE with wildcards on both sides, which cannot seek a B-tree index, so the database scans. `StartsWith` can seek. For real search, use full-text search or a dedicated search index.
questions.asked: Search boxes are in every CRUD app; interviewers want to hear about scans and alternatives.

questions.q: What SQL shape does EF Core produce for this query?
questions.code:
db.Orders.GroupBy(o => o.CustomerId)
  .Select(g => new { g.Key, Total = g.Sum(o => o.Total) })
choices: A plain SELECT of every order, grouped afterwards in memory
One query per customer, each summing that customer's orders
A `GROUP BY CustomerId` with `SUM(Total)` in a single query
A window function that returns every order with a running total
questions.why: GroupBy followed by aggregates in the projection translates to `GROUP BY` with `SUM`, so only one row per customer comes back. Aggregating in SQL avoids moving every order across the network.
questions.asked: Reporting endpoints depend on aggregates running in the database.

questions.q: What does `EnableSensitiveDataLogging()` add to EF Core's logs, and where should it be used?
choices: Parameter values and data in messages; development only
Stack traces for every query; production only, for support
Connection string passwords; staging only, when debugging
Query timings for each query; everywhere, as it costs nothing
questions.why: By default EF logs SQL with parameter values hidden. This option shows values (and entity key values in exceptions), which may include personal data or secrets, so keep it to development. Timings are logged regardless.
questions.asked: Checks you balance debuggability with data protection.

questions.q: How many times does this code query the database?
choices: Once, because EF caches the result of the first execution
Three times, once for each operator that executes the query
Twice, because Count and ToList share one round trip
Once, when the `open` variable is first assigned
questions.why: An `IQueryable` is a query definition, not a result. Each executing call runs its own SQL. Sometimes that is right (a count query is cheaper than loading rows); if you need the rows anyway, materialise once and count in memory.
questions.asked: Multiple enumeration is a subtle cost; this checks you know when queries run.

questions.q: An export endpoint must process a million rows without loading them all into memory. Which approach fits?
choices: `ToListAsync()`, then loop over the list and release it at the end
`AsNoTracking().AsAsyncEnumerable()` with `await foreach`
`Skip/Take` pages of one row each, in a tight loop until empty
`FindAsync` for each id from 1 to the highest id in the table
questions.why: `AsAsyncEnumerable` streams rows from the data reader as you iterate, and no tracking stops the context from holding every entity. `ToListAsync` buffers everything first, and row-at-a-time queries make a million round trips.
questions.asked: Large exports are a real task; streaming shows you think about memory.

questions.q: Does this query work in EF Core 3+ where `FormatLabel` is a plain C# method?
choices: No: any untranslatable method in a query throws an exception
Yes, but the Where clause is also run in memory as a result
No, unless FormatLabel is marked with a `[DbFunction]` attribute
Yes: the filter runs in SQL, and the final projection calls it in C#
questions.why: EF Core allows client evaluation only in the top-level projection, after the data is read, so this works and `Where` still runs in SQL. The same method inside `Where` or `OrderBy` would throw, because it would need all rows to evaluate.
